rationale: Start with a broad mid-strength scouting gradient at moderate temperature to spread unknown components across the full window and reveal overall retention, elution density, and any missing late peaks. This gives a balanced first map for choosing whether the next runs should be shallower, steeper, weaker, or stronger.

All 10 compounds eluted with excellent resolution, so the objective is now to cut analysis time while preserving the current separation margin. A steeper gradient should bring the late peak earlier and test how much runtime can be reduced before the closest mid-cluster pair begins to compress.

The 12 min gradient is very fast but slightly over-compresses the critical pair, so move to a slightly shallower gradient to recover resolution with minimal time penalty. This should target the sweet spot near the current optimum by selectively expanding the crowded mid-elution region.

The optimum appears very close, with 14 min just slightly under-resolving the critical pair. Increasing to 16 min should modestly expand the crowded region and is a direct test of whether full resolution can be reached while keeping the run-time penalty negligible.

Since tG 14 min is closest to optimal, keep that slope region but lower the final organic slightly to selectively retain and spread the later/mid-late cluster without adding much early retention. This probes whether the critical pair can be nudged above the threshold while avoiding the larger time penalty seen at 16 min.

You have already hit the maximum CRF, so the only useful follow-up is to test the edge of the optimum and map robustness. Shortening the gradient at the same endpoints checks whether the method can be made faster while staying on the CRF=1.0 plateau or whether the critical pair immediately drops back below the threshold.

The optimum is clearly around tG 14 min, and lowering phi1 from 0.90 to 0.85 improved the critical pair enough to reach CRF 1.000. Dropping phi1 one more step tests whether there is a broader maximum or added robustness for the critical pair without incurring a meaningful time penalty.

The best method is already at the CRF ceiling, so the next informative test is robustness in a second dimension. Lowering temperature slightly should increase retention and may further open the critical pair while showing whether the optimum at 40 C sits on a narrow or broad operating plateau.

The temperature test showed strong selectivity sensitivity, with 35 C causing a new coelution, so probe the opposite direction. Raising T to 45 C will map whether 40 C is truly the apex or whether a slightly higher temperature preserves full resolution and possibly broadens method robustness.

Temperature robustness is poor, so return to 40 C and test robustness in starting strength instead. Increasing phi0 slightly while keeping the successful endpoint and slope region will show whether the optimum depends critically on the weak initial hold or whether similar selectivity can be retained with a stronger, potentially more practical start.

A stronger starting composition at phi0 0.15 retained the maximum CRF and slightly shortened the run, so test one more step higher to define the robustness limit on the fast side. This will show whether the method remains on the CRF=1 plateau or begins to compress the earliest and critical mid-cluster separations.

Phi0 0.15 remains on the CRF ceiling while giving a slightly faster method than phi0 0.10, so keep that stronger start and test a slightly shallower gradient for extra resolution margin. This checks whether a more robust operating point exists near the optimum without incurring enough time to hurt the score.

With several CRF=1.000 methods identified, the most useful remaining mapping is the upper phi1 edge at the faster phi0 0.15 start. This tests whether the optimum plateau spans higher final organic or whether phi1 0.85 is a sharp selectivity maximum for the critical pair.

Phi1 mapping at phi0 0.15 shows 0.90 slightly worsens the critical pair versus 0.85, so test the lower side to bracket the plateau symmetrically. This will confirm whether phi1 0.85 is the true center of the optimum or whether the maximum extends toward weaker final organic.

The best-performing composition is now well mapped in phi0/phi1/tG, and temperature has shown strong selectivity effects near 35–45 C. Testing 30 C defines the lower-temperature boundary of robustness for the optimum composition and helps characterize whether the CRF=1 region is narrowly centered at 40 C or changes more gradually below it.

Temperature mapping confirms 40 C is the clear optimum, so explore the remaining composition boundary at that temperature. Lowering phi0 to 0.05 tests whether the CRF=1 plateau extends to a weaker start or whether the best region is centered near phi0 0.10–0.15.

A useful remaining question is whether the selectivity loss at lower temperature can be offset by a steeper gradient that redistributes the crowded central cluster. This checks for a compensating interaction between temperature and gradient slope while staying close to the best-performing composition window.

The lower-temperature/steeper-gradient test did not recover selectivity, so probe the opposite side to see whether higher temperature combined with a steeper gradient shifts the critical overlap behavior. This will complete the temperature–slope interaction map around the best composition using a fast method variant.

The key unresolved boundary near the optimum is how far the method can be pushed toward faster, stronger-start conditions before the critical pair fails. This combines the two directions that individually moved toward the limit but stayed close to the optimum, giving a sharp robustness test on the fast edge of the CRF plateau.

You already know 0.15/0.85/14 and 0.10/0.85/14 reach CRF 1.000, and the remaining gap is whether a weaker phi1 can support the faster 12 min gradient at phi0 0.15. This tests whether the improved margin seen at phi1 0.80 for tG 14 translates into a faster CRF=1 method or still falls just short.

The remaining unexplored corner near the fast boundary is whether the weaker start at phi0 0.10 can recover enough separation for a 12 min gradient when paired with the lower phi1 0.80. This completes the local map around the best region and tests for any unexpectedly faster near-optimum condition.

The CRF=1 region is bracketed on the low and moderate phi0 side, but the stronger-start limit has only been tested up to phi0 0.20. Pushing to phi0 0.25 at the best phi1/tG/T maps the upper robustness boundary and shows how quickly the early and critical-pair separations collapse beyond the optimum plateau.

The optimum plateau is established at 14 min, and 12 min is just beyond the fast edge, so the most informative remaining test is to map the failure rate further inside the same neighborhood. A 10 min gradient at the best composition will define how sharply the critical cluster collapses as runtime is pushed shorter.

To separate the effects of shorter gradient time from stronger starting strength, test the same fast 10 min gradient at the weaker phi0 0.10 start. This will show whether the critical-pair collapse at 10 min is intrinsic to the slope or can be partly rescued by a weaker initial composition.

For the final run, map the remaining untested combination adjacent to the optimum where both stronger phi0 and lower phi1 may counterbalance each other. This closes the local design space around the best region and tests whether a second CRF=1 plateau point exists on the faster, stronger-start side.
